learningObjectives.title: Specific heat capacity and latent heat

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates density, mass and volume?
questions.explain: Density is defined as mass per unit volume, so ρ = m ÷ V.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explain: Density is mass (kg) divided by volume (m³), giving units of kg/m³.

questions.q: A metal block has a mass of 300 kg and a volume of 0.15 m³. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass ÷ volume = 300 ÷ 0.15 = 2000 kg/m³.

questions.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
options: Its particles are arranged in an open structure so the same mass takes up more volume
Its particles have more mass than water particles
Its particles move faster than in liquid water
questions.explain: In ice the particles form an open lattice, increasing volume for the same mass and so lowering density.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from a solid to a liquid?
questions.explain: Melting is the change of state from solid to liquid.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from a gas to a liquid?
questions.explain: Condensation is the change of state from gas to liquid.

questions.q: Why is a change of state described as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
options: The mass is conserved and the original substance can be recovered
New substances are formed during the change
The mass increases as the state changes
The chemical bonds within molecules are broken permanently
questions.explain: In a change of state no new substance forms, mass is conserved and the change is reversible, so it is physical.

questions.q: While a pure solid is melting, its temperature stays constant. Why?
options: The energy supplied is used to break the bonds between particles rather than raise the temperature
No energy is being supplied during melting
The particles stop moving completely while melting
The thermometer cannot read changing temperatures
questions.explain: During melting the supplied energy increases the particles' potential energy by breaking bonds, so the temperature does not rise.

questions.q: What is the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C
The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance
The temperature at which the substance changes state
The energy stored in 1 kg of the substance
questions.explain: Specific heat capacity is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K).

questions.q: Which equation gives the change in thermal energy when a substance is heated without changing state?
options: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature
change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat
change in thermal energy = mass ÷ specific heat capacity
change in thermal energy = specific heat capacity × change in temperature
questions.explain: The thermal energy change is ΔQ = m × c × Δθ.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C)
A substance has a high specific heat capacity. What does this mean when it is heated?
options: It requires a large amount of energy to change its temperature
It changes state at a low temperature
questions.explain: A high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise, so it heats up slowly.

questions.q: What is the specific latent heat of a substance?
options: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance with no change in temperature
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C
The temperature at which a substance boils
The mass of substance changed by 1 J of energy
questions.explain: Specific latent heat is the energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

questions.q: Which equation gives the thermal energy needed for a change of state?
options: thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat
thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature
thermal energy = mass ÷ specific latent heat
thermal energy = specific latent heat ÷ mass
questions.explain: For a change of state, Q = m × L, where L is the specific latent heat.

questions.q: For a given substance, how does the specific latent heat of vaporisation compare with the specific latent heat of fusion?
options: The latent heat of vaporisation is larger
The latent heat of fusion is larger
The latent heat of fusion is always zero
questions.explain: Boiling requires separating particles completely, needing more energy per kilogram than melting, so vaporisation has the larger latent heat.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg)
How does a gas exert pressure on the walls of its container?
options: Its particles collide with the walls, each collision exerting a small force
Its particles stick to the walls and pull them inwards
Its particles dissolve into the walls
The gas particles expand to fill the gaps in the walls
questions.explain: Gas pressure results from the many collisions of fast-moving particles with the container walls, each exerting a small force.

questions.q: A fixed volume of gas is heated. Why does its pressure increase?
options: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
The particles become larger and take up more space
The particles stop moving and press on the walls
questions.explain: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so collisions with the walls are more frequent and forceful, raising the pressure.

questions.q: The temperature of a gas is directly related to which property of its particles?
questions.explain: The temperature of a gas is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles.

questions.q: A gas is at a temperature of 27 °C. What is this temperature in kelvin?
questions.explain: To convert to kelvin, add 273: 27 + 273 = 300 K.
